Record date: 2130-02-04
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 02/04/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Continued shortness of breath, increased sputum production, and persistent fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit two days after his last evaluation. Since the initiation of Piperacillin-tazobactam therapy, the patient reports a slight improvement in his respiratory symptoms. He notes that the frequency of his cough has decreased, although he continues to produce sputum, which remains yellowish-green. Mr. Fairfax mentions that he feels less fatigued but still experiences significant shortness of breath, especially with activities such as walking to the bathroom.
The patient denies any new chills or night sweats but reports occasional mild fevers, which he attributes to his ongoing infection. He has been compliant with his medication regimen, including the increased supplemental oxygen, and continues to utilize his nebulizer as prescribed. Gastrointestinal symptoms remain stable, with no significant changes noted.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + mild fatigue, - night sweats, - chills, + intermittent low-grade fever. Pulmonary - + productive cough with yellow-green sputum, + dyspnea, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, - stable heartburn, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/82 mmHg - Heart Rate: 88 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 26 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 82% on supplemental oxygen (15 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued but is in less severe respiratory distress compared to the previous visit.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Persistent wheezing on auscultation; diminished breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; crackles noted throughout lung fields, particularly in the lower lobes.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort noted; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with ongoing bacterial infection, likely related to Pseudomonas aeruginosa; sputum color remains concerning. 2. Continued improvement in respiratory status, but significant dyspnea persists; current antibiotic therapy appears to be partially effective. 3. Fatigue remains impactful, although there is a slight improvement in overall energy levels; gastrointestinal symptoms stable.
PLAN
1. Continue Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours intravenously; reassess efficacy in 48 hours and adjust based on clinical response and culture results. 2. Maintain oral Prednisone at 60 mg daily with tapering plans contingent upon clinical improvement; continue Omeprazole at 40 mg daily. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 20 L via nasal cannula; monitor closely for any signs of respiratory distress or hypoxemia. 4. Schedule a repeat chest X-ray to evaluate for any new complications; if no improvement is noted, consider bronchoscopy for further evaluation. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed and maintain Ipratropium bromide therapy. 6. Schedule follow-up visit in 48 hours to reassess respiratory function, sputum characteristics, and overall clinical condition; consider referral to pulmonology if no significant improvement.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax will remain under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to monitor his clinical status, particularly focusing on respiratory function and infection management. Patient education will be reinforced regarding the importance of adherence to the treatment regimen and the need to report any new or worsening symptoms, particularly related to respiratory function or changes in sputum production.
